newsitem.title: GERMANY: Slow German growth pushes unemployment up.
newsitem.headline: Slow German growth pushes unemployment up.

text.p: German unemployment rose sharply in September, as economic growth is still too low to boost the jobs market, Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said on Tuesday.
The number of jobless rose 39,000 to 4.0 million on a seasonally adjusted basis. The adjusted unemployment rate edged up to 10.4 percent from 10.3 percent, the Bundesbank said.
On an unadjusted basis, the number of jobless fell to 3.8 million from 3.9 million.
"The improvement (in the unadjusted data) was relatively weak due to too-low economic growth," Jagoda said. "We have not yet felt growth impulses from the economy in the jobs market."
"I can't yet see any significant turnaround," Jagoda told a news conference, adding that there could be a slight improvement in October, but nothing dramatic.
Economists, who pay much closer attention to the adjusted unemployment data, were not expecting such a sharp rise in joblessness and began to question the speed of recovery.
"This is certainly a setback for hopes that the economy is gaining momentum," Deutsche Bank senior economist Rainer Veit told Reuters Financial Television.

The German economy rebounded to 1.2 percent annual economic growth in the second quarter from 0.2 percent in the first quarter, but the government still forecasts growth of just 0.75 to 1 percent for the full year.
The weak unemployment data alone would not be enough to convince the Bundesbank to lower its securities repurchase rate, the central bank's key "repo," economists said.
But most economists agreed that the continued slump on the jobs front would cause the central bank to take a hard look at the economy and the state of recovery.
The rise in unemployment reflected uncertainty by companies about making new investments, said Barclays de Zoete Wedd economist Mathias Haffner.
"It looks like companies are still very reluctant to hire new people, possibly also because of the insecurity with relation to changes in labour legislation, for example in sick-pay," he said.
